conversation.content:
Hi there, I’m Dr. Martinez, a clinician who specializes in helping new mothers adjust emotionally after childbirth. Thank you for taking a few minutes today—I know your hands are full.

We’re going to use a short questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS. It’s simply a way to check in on how you’ve been feeling emotionally over the past seven days, so we can be sure you’re getting the support you deserve. Everything you share is confidential, and this is a judgment-free space. There are ten gentle questions; we’ll go one at a time, and you can answer in your own words. Ready when you are.

To start: **Over the last seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?**

Yeah… most of the time I can still laugh. My husband will make a silly joke while he’s changing her diaper and I’ll crack a smile. It’s not quite the same belly-laugh I used to have, but I do still find things funny sometimes.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yes, most days I can still laugh—maybe not as hard as before, but I do notice the funny moments.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I’ve looked forward to a few things—like taking the baby out in the stroller when the weather’s nice—but the excitement isn’t quite the same. I still enjoy my morning coffee and catching up with my best friend on FaceTime, yet I don’t feel that same spark of “can’t-wait” like I used to.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Sometimes, yeah. Like yesterday when she wouldn’t nap and kept crying—I kept thinking maybe I’m not doing the “right” routine, or that I missed some cue. I know rationally babies just have rough days, but I still catch myself wondering if it’s my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

A couple of times this week I’ll just be sitting on the couch, everything quiet, and suddenly my chest feels tight—like I’m waiting for something bad to happen even though nothing’s wrong. It passes if I get up and do the dishes or focus on the baby, but it pops up out of nowhere.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
Not really panicky—just that little flutter of worry I mentioned. It’s more like a nagging “what if” than a full-blown scare.
Things have been getting on top of me
Some days, yeah. When she’s fussy and the laundry’s piled up, I feel like I’m drowning a little. I usually take a breath and chip away at it, but it’s stressful in the moment.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, sleeping’s actually been okay. I’m tired, but once I lie down I drift off pretty quickly.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… I do feel kind of down some days. Nothing huge—just this heavy, blah feeling that sits on me, especially in the evenings when the house gets quiet. It’s not crying-in-the-corner sad, more like a gray cloud that follows me around for a few hours.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

I cried twice this week—once when she wouldn’t latch and I felt stuck on the couch, and again yesterday when I dropped a whole plate of spaghetti on the floor. It wasn’t really about the food; I just felt overwhelmed for a minute and the tears came.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I’m tired and stressed, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself.

You've shared that over the past week you can still laugh and enjoy small pleasures like coffee or a stroll with your baby, yet you've noticed a definite dip in enthusiasm and a nagging sense of heaviness most evenings. You described sudden episodes of chest-tightening worry, moments of self-blame when your daughter is fussy, and feeling momentarily "drowned" by chores. You cried twice, quickly felt overwhelmed, but you are sleeping when the baby allows and you firmly deny any thoughts of self-harm.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 12, Risk Level: High possibility of depression (concerns include <sym>Patient enjoys a few activities but explicitly states the excitement is diminished, matching "Definitely less than I used to"</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly reports "sometimes" blaming herself and gives a clear recent example, aligning with "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, unexplained anxiety episodes occurring multiple times in the past week, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>She reports feeling overwhelmed "some days" and "like I'm drowning," indicating intermittent difficulty coping, aligning with the option "Yes, sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual."</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total of 12 places you above the 11-point threshold that signals high likelihood of <med>perinatal depression</med>. You endorse <sym>diminished interest</sym> (<quote>spark isn't quite the same</quote>), <sym>daily low mood</sym> (<quote>gray cloud</quote>), <sym>unwarranted guilt</sym>, <sym>multiple anxiety episodes</sym>, and <sym>crying spells</sym>, all within two weeks post-birth, meeting core <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. <sym>Absence of suicidal ideation</sym> is reassuring yet does not negate clinical concern. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange an appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> within the next week to review these results and consider treatment options
2. Request routine <med>thyroid</med> and <med>anemia</med> labs to rule out medical contributors to mood symptoms
3. Plan a follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks to track progress
4. Incorporate 15-20 minutes of gentle outdoor walking most days; evidence shows light movement reduces <sym>postpartum depressive symptoms</sym>
5. Share your feelings with a trusted adult daily; brief emotional check-ins lower <sym>stress hormone</sym> levels
6. Limit daily chores to one priority task; ask partner or friend to handle extras while you recover
7. Keep your baby nearby at night but try alternating one bottle of expressed milk/formula so you can obtain a 4-5 hour stretch of sleep at least twice weekly
8. If low mood, anxiety, or crying worsens or you ever think of self-harm, call the <med>national maternal mental health hotline</med> (1-833-943-5746) or local emergency services immediately
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 12: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – Brief Summary

Symptoms & Observations
- Low mood: endorses “gray,” heavy feelings most evenings
- Anhedonia: reduced anticipatory pleasure; still enjoys coffee & brief calls, yet “spark” diminished
- Excessive guilt: self-blame when infant is fussy, despite rational insight
- Anxiety: episodic chest tightness, free-floating worry several times per week; no frank panic
- Overwhelm: “drowning” sensation when chores & infant needs coincide; uses task-breakdown to cope
- Crying spells: twice this week after minor stressors; linked to feeling stuck/overloaded
- Sleep: no difficulty initiating sleep; tiredness attributed to infant care

Pattern
Mild-moderate depressive features with co-occurring generalized anxiety; no suicidal ideation reported.

Risk Factors Present
- Persistent low mood and crying
- Partial anhedonia
- Maladaptive guilt
- Unprompted anxious arousal
- Perceived functional overload

Safety Screening
Denies thoughts of self-harm; no further safety concerns identified.

Screening Class
Elevated scores consistent with possible postpartum depression ± anxiety; formal diagnostic evaluation recommended.
